summary: This RFC specifies how to packetize KLV Encoded Data, as defined in SMPTE ST 336, into RTP.

plainLanguage.summary: Video files carry small labelled data bits. This explains how to send those bits across a network in packets.

questions: how is klv carried over rtp
subtitle: How to carry SMPTE KLV metadata, the labelled data that travels with video, inside RTP packets.

tldr.problem: SMPTE ST 336 defines a byte-level Key-Length-Value encoding for metadata that goes with video, but says nothing about sending it over an RTP stream.
tldr.mechanism: KLV items that share a presentation time are grouped into a KLVunit and placed in one or more RTP packets, with no payload header. All packets of a unit share one timestamp, and the marker bit flags the packet holding the unit's last byte.
tldr.outcome: Any KLV data can be streamed over RTP, and a receiver can find unit boundaries and spot damaged units after packet loss using only the marker bit and sequence numbers.

today: RFC 6597 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of this payload format.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6597 specifies how to packetize KLV (Key-Length-Value) encoded data, as defined by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers in SMPTE ST 336, into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550).

The format is built so that arbitrary KLV data can be carried. No restrictions are placed on which KLV data keys can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a set of rules for putting small labelled notes about a video into network packets. Any kind of note is allowed.

sections.title: KLV and SMPTE ST 336
sections.content:
SMPTE ST 336 defines a byte-level data encoding for data items and data groups, independent of the application or transport. A KLV triplet has a Key that identifies the data, a Length that gives its size, and a Value that is the data itself.

The Key is a fixed-length 16-byte SMPTE-administered Universal Label. Its structure is described in SMPTE ST 298, and keys are kept in registries published by SMPTE. The RFC says this encoding has been used for metadata that describes or enhances video presentations.

KLV triplets can be combined into sets that are themselves KLV coded: the full form (Universal Sets) or one of four more compact forms (Global Sets, Local Sets, Variable Length Packs and Defined Length Packs). KLV can also carry information registered with a non-SMPTE external agency.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note is a labelled box: a name tag, a size, and the contents. Boxes can be packed inside bigger boxes to save space.

sections.title: KLVunits and the RTP Header
sections.content:
The design goal is simple but robust carriage of all forms of ST 336 data. It stays simple by using only the standard RTP headers and defining no payload headers.

The data is split into KLVunits: the logical collection of all KLV items to be presented at a specific time. A unit is one or more KLV items, one after another with no padding or stuffing. Compound items such as sets and packs are allowed, but their contents MUST NOT be split across two KLVunits.

Two RTP header fields get special use. The timestamp gives the instant on the presentation timeline at which the whole KLVunit is presented, and its clock frequency is a payload format parameter. The marker bit (M) is set to 1 on any packet that contains the final byte of a KLVunit and to 0 on all other packets. All other header fields are used as in RFC 3550.
sections.plainLanguage: All notes meant for the same moment go in one bundle. Every packet of a bundle gets the same time stamp, and the last packet gets a flag saying it is the end.

sections.title: Mapping a KLVunit to Packets
sections.content:
An RTP payload SHALL contain one, and only one, KLVunit or a fragment of one. Packet size is up to the implementation, which should consider limits such as the MTU. A small unit goes directly into one payload, so the first payload byte is the first byte of a Universal Label Key.

A unit too large for one packet MAY span several. Its data MUST be sent in sequential byte order, so that putting the packets in sequence number order and joining their payloads exactly reproduces the original unit. All of those packets MUST carry the same timestamp.

Because the marker bit flags the last packet, a receiver can hand a unit to the decoder as soon as that packet arrives. Without it, the receiver would have to wait for a packet with a different timestamp to learn that the unit had ended.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bundle is too big for one envelope, you split it across several in order, with the same time stamp on each. The last envelope is marked so the reader knows to stop.

sections.title: Lost Packets and Damaged KLVunits
sections.content:
Packet loss can lose whole KLVunits or parts of them. Lost packets are detected through the RTP sequence number. A receiver MUST treat two groups as damaged KLVunits: the unit partially received before the lost packet (back to, but not including, the latest packet with M set to 1), and the first unit received after the lost packet (the first packet after the loss and, if its M bit is 0, all following packets up to and including the next with M set to 1).

This applies whatever the lost packet's own M bit was, so very basic receivers can find the outer bounds of damaged units by looking only at the M bit.

What to do with a damaged unit is left to each implementation. KLV streams allow partial recovery, but because some implementations are limited, receivers MAY drop damaged units entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: If an envelope goes missing, the bundle it belonged to and the bundle right after it might be incomplete. The reader may throw those bundles away or try to save what it can.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP
sections.content:
The payload format uses the media type application/smpte336m. Its one required parameter is rate, the RTP timestamp clock rate, typically chosen from the sampling rate of the metadata. There are no optional parameters.

The type is framed and binary and is defined only for transfer via RTP. Receivers might understand only some data items, and unrecognized items are skipped, so which items are used is typically agreed out of band. SDP mapping follows Section 3 of RFC 4855. The format has no configuration or optional format parameters, so Offer/Answer and declarative use raise no special considerations. IANA registered the media type.
sections.plainLanguage: The format has a name tag, and the only thing you must say when using it is how fast its clock ticks.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content:
The usual RTP concerns apply: confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. No single mechanism fits every case, but SRTP is recommended if suitable; IPsec and TLS are named as other options.

Because KLV item lengths are essentially unbounded, it is easy to build data that makes a naive decoder allocate large resources, a denial-of-service threat. Receivers SHOULD limit resource allocation within the bounds of any application profile in use. The format has no inherently active content, but individual KLV items could be defined to carry some. Accepting such content from streams without authenticity or integrity protection exposes receivers to spoofed-packet attacks. Receivers that cannot decode such items are not at risk, since unknown items are skipped.

For congestion control, the general RTP rules apply. ST 336 grouping constructs such as local sets and data packs can reduce bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could send a fake note claiming to be enormous to make the reader run out of room. So readers set limits, and it is wise to lock the packets so only trusted senders get through.
